issues.legal_issue: The proof of legal necessity required to sustain an alienation of joint-family property does not require proof that every part of the consideration was applied to family needs.
material_facts: A father who managed the joint family sold joint-family property for consideration of Rs. 50,000.
The evidence established that Rs. 45,000 was required for family purposes, including debts, public demands and marriages; necessity was not established for the remaining amount.
issues.conclusion: The sale was supported by legal necessity and was binding on the family; the alienee was not required to prove the application of every part of the consideration.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, an alienee must establish legal necessity for the transaction, but need not establish that every part of the consideration was actually applied to family needs. Sri Krishan Das v. Nathu Ram and Niamat Rai v. Din Dayal were relied on.

rule.if: joint_family_sale_challenge and manager_sold_family_property and transaction_need_established and some_consideration_application_unproved

predicates.joint_family_sale_challenge: The proceeding seeks to set aside a sale of joint-family property.
predicates.manager_sold_family_property: The person managing the family sold its property.
predicates.transaction_need_established: The evidence showed that a substantial part of the consideration was required for family purposes.
predicates.some_consideration_application_unproved: The evidence did not establish that every part of the consideration was applied to family purposes.

issues.definition: When a challenge to a manager's sale shows that the transaction was supported by family need despite some unproved application of consideration, the sale binds the family.

issues.legal_issue: A necessary alienation executed by a family manager can bind a minor family member even when that minor also joined in executing the sale deed.
material_facts: The father was the manager of the joint family and executed the sale deed for family purposes, including expressly on behalf of a minor son.
The appellant had also signed the deed while described as a major, but was in fact a minor.
The transaction was supported by family needs.
issues.conclusion: The father's execution as manager made the transaction binding on the minor's interest; the minor's joining as an executant did not affect that result.
issues.legal_principle: A family manager competent to bind the family may make an alienation binding on the interests of all family members when the transaction is supported by legal necessity. The junior member's participation does not prevent the manager from acting for the family. Gharib-Ullah v. Khalak Singh, Kanti Chunder Goswami v. Bisheswar Goswami, and Biraj Nopani v. Pura Sundary Dasee were relied on.

rule.if: joint_family_alienation_challenge and family_manager_executed_for_family and transaction_supported_by_family_need and minor_member_joined_as_executant

predicates.joint_family_alienation_challenge: The proceeding challenges an alienation of joint-family property.
predicates.family_manager_executed_for_family: The person managing the family executed the transaction on behalf of the family.
predicates.transaction_supported_by_family_need: The evidence showed that the transaction was required for family purposes.
predicates.minor_member_joined_as_executant: A family member who was a minor also signed the transaction.

issues.definition: When a family manager executes an alienation for family purposes and a minor family member also signs it, the manager's transaction binds that minor's interest.

issues.legal_issue: A deed transferring sir land together with all rights and privileges expressly transfers the cultivating right in that land even if it does not name that right separately.
material_facts: The sale deed transferred sir and khudkashat lands, cultivated and uncultivated lands, together with all rights and privileges.
The deed did not separately name the cultivating rights in the sir lands.
The dispute concerned whether those cultivating rights passed to the purchasers.
issues.conclusion: The deed expressly transferred the cultivating rights in the sir lands, so the transferors did not retain those rights.
issues.legal_principle: Section 49(1) of the C. P. Tenancy Act, 1920, requires an express agreement to transfer the right to cultivate sir land; a transfer by implication is insufficient. The words conveying the lands with all rights and privileges expressly included the cultivating rights, and the deed must be read so that those words are given effect.

predicates.sir_land_transfer_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a transfer of sir land included the right to cultivate it.
predicates.deed_transfers_sir_land: The transferor conveyed sir land to the transferee.
predicates.deed_conveys_land_with_all_rights_and_pr: The deed conveyed the land together with all rights and privileges relating to it.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns transferred sir land and the deed conveys it with all associated rights and privileges, the cultivating right is transferred.
